newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania labour unions slam government over reforms.
newsitem.headline: Romania labour unions slam government over reforms.

text.p: Romania's biggest labour unions walked out of talks with Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea on Thursday, accusing the coalition government of botching market reforms.

Labour leaders, who have so far backed President Emil Constantinescu's administration, urged him to defuse the conflict, one of the biggest challenges it has faced since defeating ex-communists last year.

The row embarrassed the government, which is trying to win approval from a visiting International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission for the disbursement of the second of five $86 million tranches of a $430 million credit programme aimed at underpinning reforms.

A cabinet session to discuss a revised 1997 budget, a key provision for IMF credits, was postponed until Friday. Ministers are at loggerheads over proposed cuts in budget allocations and scarce revenue from slow privatisation.

Trade unionists accused the goverment of proceeding too slowly with reform and doing nothing to halt bickering among ministers. They said they would not return to the talks unless Constantinescu also took part.

"The present government crisis is extremely harmful for economic and social life," said a statement issued by the National Trade Union (BNS) bloc which, together with three other unions in attendance, have a membership of four million.
Ciorbea dismissed calls for dismissals. The state Rompres news agency said he blamed discord in the government coalition on "lack of communication, or even childish attitudes".
He had scheduled several meetings this week with the trade unionists, seeking to allay fears of mass job cuts as Romania sets about shutting down bloated communist-era plants.
The independent news agency said the final straw for the union leaders was a government proposal to switch the agenda away from their proposals for wage indexation and tax cuts.
It said BNS leader Dumitru Costin urged Ciorbea to sack Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu and junior finance officials, over accusations of incompetence, or to resign himself.

The Fund mission, in Romania until next week, has yet to comment on the government's progress in curbing inflation, proceeding with stalled privatisation and closing down inefficient farms and industries.
Ciorbea told reporters he had been "negotiating with the IMF representatives for 10 to 12 hours a day, because we have a big volume of work to cover".

Constantinescu, who defeated ex-communist Ion Iliescu in last year's election, appointed Ciorbea to head a government of Christian Democrats, Liberals, Social Democrats and members of the 1.6 million-strong ethnic Hungarian community.
It has liberalised prices, freed foreign exchange markets and introduced legislation to attract foreign investors.

Ministers say monthly inflation, which peaked at more than 30 percent in March, will slide below two percent in July and have pledged to stick to keep the 1997 budget deficit within a target of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product.
